body.head: Theatrical Examiner
body.p: On Monday last was born of the exhausted muse of Mr. Thomas Dibdin an opera called Up to Town, and on the Thursday following the abortion died. We hope that this will be the last of this gentleman's attempts at dramatic composition: the task requires higher powers and attainments than he possesses; and if criticism had always done its duty so honestly, as it did upon the present occasion, Mr. T. Dibdin would never have been the successful writer which the Managers of Theatres may deem him; for even the Morning Post condemned the opera of Up to Town. The opera is now defunct; so that our criticism must be free from all accusations of indignant and vindictive spirit: we can have no quarrel with the dead. Up to Town was most certainly in one word bad; but we do not think it was worse than the author's former successful compositions of a similar nature: it was as a whole most unequivocally dull; but not duller than the Cabinet without its music, the English Fleet, or Family Quarrels. On the contrary, we think there was much more good intention in it, than in any of those operas. The first act was occupied with village life; the coming of the post, the consequential airs of the post-master (Mr. Liston), a well-acted farmer by Mr. Emery, and a really good farewell-scene between an old nurse (Mrs. Davenport) and her daughter (Miss S. Booth), previously to the sweeting's coming Up to Town, in which the gossip advises her to beware of pride, and not notice the London footmen, to take care of her morals, and buy her mother some warm gingerbread in Threadneedle-street,—gave an interest and pleasantry to the feelings, which was certainly not sustained by the remaining two acts. There the scene was laid in London; and the second act opened with a well-contrasted drawing-room, in which a fashionable couple (Mr. Jones and Mrs. Childe) were seen reproaching each other with their respective expenses,—the husband indignant at his wife's having sold his greys to pay her milliner, while it comes out at last that the husband has previously parted with the wife's little cottage ornée to pay his stable-keeper. We had seen many worse-managed scenes than this. There was a good deal of drollery in Mr. Fawcett's caricature of an Attorney, who passed his mornings in Chancery-lane, and his evenings at Chelsea, whose clerk was equally dexterous at copying a conveyance or cultivating a cauliflower, and who entered the stage in a suit of legal black and a surtout of pea-green, with a nolle prosequi in one hand and a nosegay in the other. But the opera certainly failed for want of plot: the nodus of the piece depended upon two equivoques which were most unnaturally set on foot, and most unhappily carried through; and although Mr. Thomas Dibdin made a few sketches of character which were not despicable, yet whenever he had sent one of his actors off the stage with a quibble, he was apt to think the man had made an exit with flying colours. There was a good deal of trumpery sentiment too about duelling, which betrayed Mr. Dibdin’s old propensity to clap-trap; but we will do him the justice to say, that he crammed no loyalty down our throats. Upon the whole, had the opera been provided with better music than that of Messrs. Reeve, Condell, Whitaker and Welsh, it would have merited quite equal success with the majority of this dramatist's former productions; but the melodies were extremely common-place, and no pretension was made to harmony, for the first two acts were without finales,—a most injudicious deficiency; since there is nothing which sends off a mediocre dialogue with more spirit than a quintett or a chorus. An opera is not opera without these things; and we recollect none such in Up to Town. The principal secret however of the failure of this piece, contrasted with the success of former ones that were no better or still worse, is to be found in the increasing spirit of newspaper criticism and in the exhausted patience of the town. The daily journals have at length begun to think for themselves in this matter, and to speak aloud for the public; and if they continue their long-desired and humane endeavours, they will soon see how much they can effect in behalf of that unfortunate lady, the British Drama, who has been in a laughing fit of the most idiotical and enfeebling description ever since the birth of O’Keefe.

The melodies allotted to Mr. Sinclair in Up to Town, were wholly unsuitable to his powers, which are very ill-calculated for hunting-songs, and such boisterous compositions. The character of this gentleman's delightful voice is, that it is always music,—clear, perfect, exquisite music; but it is a stream, not a fall, of waters; a crystal fountain welling away through summer gardens and soothing the ear with delicious attention; not a torrent, to go headlong over crags and precipices, and deafen and turn us giddy. Neither are Mrs. Childe's powers strong; but there is a delicacy about her voice and manner which will always ensure the satisfaction of an audience. Miss Feron has had trial enough at our hands. She has an excellent voice, but a most uncultivated one: she cannot shake, and she slurs all her divisions, in the hopes of astonishing by their rapidity, rather than delighting by their correctness. Her figure is extremely petite, and she is constantly swelling herself on tip-toe, and giving herself all the airs of those tragedy heroines, in which she may have grown so great at the Circus. Her language is full of vulgarisms; and, whether we consider her as an actress, a speaker, or a singer, we must say to her, "To school; to school; to school."

Let not the public suppose that it was the disapprobation of the audience on each night of the performance of this Opera, or the vituperation of the daily critics, that procured the withdrawment of the piece, so much as the comparative emptiness of the houses. After the play-bills had been constantly underlined with the success and applause of this Opera, it was stated to the malcontents on Thursday evening, that the Managers, "bowing to their decision," would withdraw the piece. To what decision? To the decision which the play-bills had all the week stated to be most favourable? See into what a dilemma these dishonourable, canting assertions reduced the Managers. We put this to Mr. Kemble's candour and integrity, as a gentleman and a scholar.
